top_comments: I made this, fun to see my project on the front page!The main question I tend to get from hacker-types is "what are the tech specs?". The demos run on a Mac with custom software I built for projection mapping/rendering/etc. (the hand tracking uses Apple's built-in framework, which is very good), a small consumer 4k laser projector, and a basic webcam for vision.But really, this is primarily a research/design prototype - I think it's much more important to figure out what the user experience should ideally feel like, if the interactions are even plausible & desirable in the first place; and then work backwards to the technology.

Nice. This reminds me how I felt watching the first pre-iPhone multitouch demos.One small quality-of-life improvement that could be added: have the software timestamp when you say "here" and then (using a short low-FPS video buffer?) analyze the corresponding frame of video. This would eliminate the pause when you're pointing at something, waiting for the computer to respond.Alternately a low-latency speech analyzer could look for the word "here" and quickly snap a screenshot. Perhaps project a temporary dot on the surface, so the user knows they can put their hand down now?Quite the impressive demo! There's huge potential here.

Quite nice. But this imbues the house with a constant presence of the machine. A jinn which is always ready to grant your wish, but never leaves you alone, ever watching and listening. The fact that the jinn takes orders spoken in normal human language amplifies the effect quite a bit. I would have rather not have to feel such presence in my bathroom. Or bedroom. I would still be glad to be able to operate "smart" switches, and even find items. But I would rather explicitly unlock my phone, start an app, and scan the bookshelf, until a book is highlighted.OTOH this would be a great thing for non-private spaces, that are watched by security cameras 24/7 anyway. A school, a library, a clinic, an office, a workshop, a warehouse, a parking garage, maybe even a museum.Of course, trust and security are going to be major considerations. Maybe not for everyone though: people voluntarily enable various voice assistants, and even pay to order Amazon Echo.

articles.summary: Talorys – A self-hosted personal AI agent on Cloudflare's free tier

top_comments: This might sound kinda crazy, but I define “self-hosted” as something that I host myself.

For all the people complaining this isn’t self hosted, it’s open source - it’s a relatively minor tweak to replace the AI calls to point to a local model server. Everything else runs locally via wrangler. It’s less than 20 minutes of work by hand, less than a minute to ask AI to do this.It’s a weird complaint for people who supposedly like hacker culture.

Careful with Cloudflare's "free" AI tier if you use paid workers. I was never able to get an answer on why I was billed for their confusing neuron usage for stuff that should have been covered under their usage limits. Their customer support just ignored my ticket. Apparently it's a known issue that they don't give a shit based on discussions in their support Discord.

Trained a SQLite-vec database on the English language for a few days with a small qwen embedding model to add vec embeds to the db then ripped the cord on the embeddings before I started feeding my llm the proper specs for Jev and now i have a cool jeopardy generator that now doubles as a Jev clone classifier with a custom v1 endpoint for system 0 or whatever it is. Level understanding here, fun experiment though ^>^ and produces useful outputs

articles.title: Unikernels were hard. key word: were
articles.summary: Unikernels were hard. key word: were

top_comments: I've had limited adventures in embedded software and as part of that became a fan of Zephyr (http://www.zephyrproject.org) and wonder about its potential application as a unikernel.On the plus side: it's a unikernel. You compile it and your application together and get a binary. It has support for running on virtual hardware (https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/hardware/virtualizatio...) and virtio is the new bios, right?On the minus side: I think porting "traditional" software - say Nginx - to it will be agonising. And I can't make any guarantees about its performance in the same way that Alpine Linux container images are not necessarily fast.But there's an entire toolchain, debugging story, drivers etc. for something that compiles to tiny and starts up basically instantaneously. Surely that's got to be useful for something?

It’s good to see this! I’m offering a cloud service to host unikernels based on my BareMetal kernel.~$0.005 CAD/h for a small network-enabled VM with 4MiB of RAM and no disk.https://baremetal.returninfinity.com
